title: Why Names Slip
description: The Baker/baker paradox, the long road from a face to a name, and your baseline

concepts.title: How it works: the Baker/baker paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
At a party you meet two people. One tells you his surname is Baker. The other tells you she is a baker. A week later you spot both of them across a room. Which fact is still there?

Almost certainly the job. This is the Baker/baker paradox: it is much harder to recall that a person's surname is Baker than to recall that a person is a baker.1 The classic study came from McWeeny, Young, Hay and Ellis in 1987, and the effect keeps turning up. In 2022 a team at the University of Graz gave volunteers unfamiliar faces to learn, each with a surname and a profession, and replicated it once more: people were faster and more accurate in recalling professions than surnames.2

Why should the same word behave so differently? Because a job comes loaded with meaning. A baker makes bread and cakes and sells them. Mr Baker, as a name, conveys little information beyond the fact that he has a common surname.3 A name is an arbitrary label, and arbitrary labels are exactly what memory handles worst.

The second reason is the route your memory takes. In 1985 Young, Hay and Ellis had 22 people keep records of their difficulties and errors in recognising people for seven weeks, and collected 922 of them.4 From these records they built a model of how you get from a face to a name, and Bruce and Young kept the same route in their 1986 model: first the face feels familiar, then you reach who the person is, and only then, from a separate store, the name.5 Later experiments fit it. In 1997 Craigie and Hanley found that recalling a name from a face was contingent upon correctly remembering the occupation learned with it.6

So the name sits at the far end of a chain, with no shortcut from the face. That is why you can say "she works in accounts, we met at the gym" while the name stays out of reach.

concepts.title: Drill: your baseline names
concepts.contentHtml:
Before you learn a single technique, find out what your memory does with names on its own. This drill copies the design of the classic experiments: every person comes with a surname and a job, and several of the surnames are also ordinary words.

  1. Picture each person from the description, the way you would see a stranger at a party.
  2. Read each line once, about five seconds a person. No tricks: do not build images or stories on purpose.
  3. Cover the card and count backwards from 30 in threes, so you are not just holding the last line in mind.
  4. Go through the descriptions only. For each one, write down the name and the job.
  5. Score names and jobs separately. Keep both numbers: the next lesson asks you to beat the first one.
Drill Read each person once, about five seconds each, with no technique. The quiz will ask for names and jobs.
  1. A tall man with a shaved head and a gold earring: Mr Potter, a pilot
  2. A woman with grey plaits and round glasses: Mrs Hughes, a baker
  3. A young man with a ginger beard and freckles: Mr Mason, a nurse
  4. A woman with a gap between her front teeth: Ms Okafor, a plumber
  5. An old man with bushy white eyebrows: Mr Fisher, a judge
  6. A woman with short red hair and a pointed chin: Ms Cook, a vet
  7. A man with a crooked nose and a deep tan: Mr Lewis, a gardener
  8. A woman with long black hair and dimples: Mrs Shepherd, a teacher

Most people find more jobs than names: the Baker/baker paradox, inside your own head. Look at which names did survive. If Fisher or Shepherd came back, did you notice that they are also jobs? Giving a bare name some meaning is the first move of the method in the next lesson.

concepts.title: Myth check: just bad with names?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Some people are good with names and I am simply bad with them, so there is no point trying.
Reality Everyone struggles, and nearly everyone knows it. In 2020 Hargis, Whatley and Castel asked younger and older adults to rate themselves against others their age. On most items, from honesty to memory for places, people rated themselves better than average, as people usually do. The exception was remembering names, which both age groups rated as about the same as everyone else.1 The Baker/baker paradox is a property of names, not a flaw in you, and the next two lessons show name memory responding to training like any other skill.

Wait, really? Often the name never got in at all. In 1973 Brenner sat people in pairs round a table: in each pair one person read words aloud in turn and the other only listened. Afterwards the readers had diminished recall for words read by other readers shortly before their own turn, starting three words before it,2 while the listeners showed no such dip. Brenner argued that, as their turn drew near, the readers were busy anticipating their own performance.3 He called it the next-in-line effect. In 2019 a team at the University of Waterloo pointed to the everyday version: co-workers taking turns to introduce themselves may struggle to remember the names said shortly before their own introduction.4

So when a round of introductions comes your way, settle what you will say before it starts, then spend your attention on everyone else. You cannot remember a name you never heard.

tryIt: Tonight, write down the name of everyone you were introduced to this week, and beside each gap note what you do remember instead: a job, a place, a joke.

title: The Name-Face Method
description: A sound-alike for the name, a feature of the face, and one image to join them

concepts.title: How it works: name, feature, image
concepts.contentHtml:
You are introduced to a Mr Smolensky. He has a very broad nose. How will "Smolensky" still be there tomorrow?

Giving names a hook is an old idea. The Roman teacher Quintilian advised that to remember the name Fabius you should think of the famous Cunctator, or of some friend bearing the same name.1 Names such as Aper, Ursus, Naso and Crispus were especially easy, he said, since in these cases we can fix their origin in our memory.2 They meant boar, bear, long-nose and curly.3 Those Romans were lucky: their names were already words.

For everyone else, the modern version comes from the mnemonist Harry Lorayne. In a 1958 book he described seeing someone skiing on Mr Smolensky's very broad nose while taking pictures with a small camera:4 small lens ski, Smolensky. The method has three parts. Turn the name into something concrete that sounds like it, a sound-alike. Pick a prominent feature of the face. Then make one interactive image that joins the two.

In 1980 McCarty tested the parts one at a time. "Bryant" became "bride ant", the cheeks were the feature, and the image was an ant in a wedding dress running across them.5 With all three parts, people recalled 55 per cent of the names.6 Groups given only some of the parts managed 12 to 23 per cent, no better than a control group who simply repeated and spelled each name. All three components were essential.7 McCarty also found the weakest link: retrieving the interactive image.8 So make that image the part you work hardest on.

concepts.title: Drill: put names on faces
concepts.contentHtml:
It does not take long to learn. In 1978 Morris, Jones and Hampson trained students with just five of Lorayne's worked examples, and they recalled 79 per cent of names against 42 per cent for a control group.1 Go slowly at first: McCarty gave each face 30 seconds.2

  1. Get the name right. Listen, say it back, and ask for the spelling if it is unusual.
  2. Make a sound-alike. If the name is already a word, use it: Fisher, Mason, Bird. If not, break it into sounds you can picture, the sound bridge from Vivid Images: Bryant, bride ant; Hammond, ham on a mound.
  3. Pick the feature that strikes you most, on the face itself. Distinctive is better: McCarty found a feature cued less well the more often it was used in a list and better the more it stood out.3
  4. Join them in action. The sound-alike does something to the feature: the ham sits on the jaw, the ant runs across the cheeks.
  5. Judge the image. Ask yourself how pleasant or unpleasant it is. With adults averaging 65.6 years, Yesavage, Rose and Bower found in 19834 that this one extra step lifted recall after 48 hours from 15 to 32 per cent.5
  6. Review from the faces. Look at each face, find the feature, and let the image hand you the name.
Drill Give each person about thirty seconds: sound-alike, feature, image, judgement. The quiz will give you the faces and ask for the names.
  1. Mr Hammond: a heavy, square jaw
  2. Ms Lockwood: thick, curly eyebrows
  3. Mr Delaney: a long, thin nose
  4. Mrs Sandford: ears that stick out
  5. Mr Kowalski: a deep cleft in his chin
  6. Ms Fairbank: a very high forehead
  7. Mr Penrose: round, rosy cheeks
  8. Ms Ashworth: a mole above her lip

Now compare with your baseline from lesson 1. Same number of people, same kind of names; the difference is what you did with each one.

concepts.title: Myth check: the party trick
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Learn the face-name method and you will remember everyone at the next party.
Reality In conversation it often fails. In 1994 Patton trained students in the method and found that it did not improve name recall when they attempted it during real conversations.1 In 2005 Morris and colleagues held a party at the start of an academic year:2 about 40 minutes of mingling, then a sheet of the guests' photos the next day. Guests told to test themselves on names recalled 24 per cent.3 Guests told to use the imagery method recalled 12 per cent, no better than the 16 per cent of guests given no method at all. Building images takes effort and a leap of imagination,4 and a conversation will not wait.

So use the method where you have time: a seating plan, a staff page, the list of speakers before a conference. At the party itself, the next lesson's tool works better.

Wait, really? Do not pin your image to the glasses. In 2014 Carney and Levin found that hooking a name to an extra detail, such as a headband or a pipe, beat a facial feature, but only when people were tested with the same picture.5 With a different photo that no longer showed the detail, facial features won. Hats come off; noses stay.

tryIt: Pick five people from tonight's news, give each surname a sound-alike picture pinned to one feature of the face, and tomorrow name them from their faces alone.

title: Names in the Wild
description: Testing yourself mid-conversation, expanding gaps and the reversed name game

concepts.title: How it works: test, do not repeat
concepts.contentHtml:
Quintilian reported that Cyrus is believed to have known the name of every soldier in his army.1 You only need the names at one party, but you cannot write them down or snap a photo while you shake hands.

In 1978 Landauer and Bjork pointed out that in real life a new name is rarely repeated during the conversation,2 so your best move is to test yourself silently, again and again. They asked students to imagine meeting people at a cocktail party and varied when each name was tested. An expanding schedule, with tests close together at first and then further apart, beat even gaps with about the same average spacing. With faces, tests after 0, 1, 3 and 8 other items beat tests after 3, 3, 3 and 3.3

The active ingredient is retrieval: pulling the name out, not having it put in front of you again. In experiments by Morris and colleagues in 2005, practising recall led to 42 per cent of names recalled, against 17 per cent when the names were simply shown again.4 Meaning helped too. Students who thought about what each name meant as well as testing themselves recalled 70 per cent, against 45 per cent for testing alone:5 the Baker/baker lesson put to work.

Do the gaps have to expand? That is less clear than it first looked. Several later studies found no advantage over even gaps.6 What holds up is that spaced tests beat crammed ones, so test early, then leave longer and longer before the next try.

concepts.title: Drill: the reversed name game
concepts.contentHtml:
Morris and Fritz turned retrieval practice into a game for groups. In the original version each person recalls everyone before them, then adds their own name. In 2002 they reversed it: say your own name, then recall the name of the person before you, and so on back to the first.1 That way the newest, most fragile name is tested first, before it gets lost behind all the others. You can play it alone, in your head, at any gathering.

  1. Say it back at once. "Hello, Priya." In Brenner's study, readers had better recall for words they read aloud themselves than for words they only heard.2
  2. Ask one question about the name. Where is it from? How is it spelled? Thinking about meaning added to the benefit of testing.
  3. Test yourself soon, a few seconds later while it is still easy, then again after a minute or two.
  4. Each time someone new arrives, run the names backwards: newest first, back to the first person you met.
  5. Test once more before you leave, and write the names down when you get home.
Drill Eight people round a table introduce themselves in this order, each with one thing they love. After each new person, recall all the names so far, newest first. The quiz will ask for the order.
  1. Priya, sailing
  2. Tom, bees
  3. Aled, rugby
  4. Grace, jazz
  5. Kenji, baking
  6. Fatima, chess
  7. Rory, fishing
  8. Elena, opera

The hobbies come from the "elaborate" version of the game, in which each player adds one word about themselves. It worked about as well as the plain version, and players rated it a little more fun.3 It also hands you something to talk about.

concepts.title: Myth check: hearing it is enough
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth If you hear a name often enough, it will stick.
Reality Hearing is not recalling. Morris and Fritz compared their name game with a version matched for repetitions: the group leader read out the growing list of names each time, so everyone heard every name just as often. After a half-hour seminar, name game players recalled between 60 and 65 per cent of the names, against about 30 per cent for the listeners.1 Two weeks later the players still had 20 to 30 per cent and the listeners about 7.

Wait, really? Reversing the order made a real difference. In Morris and Fritz's 2002 study, people were tested three times, at 30 minutes, two weeks and eight weeks. Overall the reversed game gave 62 per cent of names, the original game 50 per cent,2 and a version in which people just read the names off the board when their turn came 32 per cent.

It scales, too: versions of the reversed game improved name learning even in groups of about 25,3 although with that many people the game can take more than half an hour. For a club, a class or a new team, that may be the best half-hour you spend all term.

tryIt: At your next gathering, say each new name back, test yourself on it a minute later and again before you leave, then write the names down at home.

title: The Keyword Method
description: Atkinson and Raugh's two links for foreign words: a sound-alike keyword and an image

concepts.title: How it works: two links to a meaning
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a word you have no way of guessing: the Russian for building is zdanie, pronounced roughly "zdon-yeh". By the end of the next paragraph it will be yours.

At Stanford University in the 1970s, Richard Atkinson and Michael Raugh tested what they called the keyword method. It splits learning a word into two links.1 The acoustic link: find an English word, the keyword, that sounds like some part of the foreign word. In zdanie you can hear "dawn". The imagery link: picture the keyword interacting with the meaning. Their suggestion was to imagine the pink light of dawn reflected in the windows of a tall building.2 For the Spanish caballo, horse, pronounced somewhat like "cob-eye-yo", the keyword is "eye": picture a giant eye winking in the forehead of a horse.

Then they gave it a hard test. Volunteers learned 120 Russian words over three days, hearing each word through headphones, with a keyword shown in brackets for the keyword group. Every day the keyword group learned more words in two study trials than the control group did in three.3 On the final test the keyword group recalled 72 per cent of the vocabulary against 46 per cent.4 Called back without warning six weeks later, they still had 43 per cent against 28.5 In a Spanish study whose control group was told to use rote rehearsal, the gap was 88 per cent to 28.6

You have met this chain before. The name-face method is the keyword method with a face in place of the meaning: Bryant becomes bride ant, and the ant goes on the cheeks.

concepts.title: Drill: eight Spanish words
concepts.contentHtml:
Good keywords are not luck. Atkinson's team had a panel choose them by three rules:1 the keyword sounds as much as possible like a part of the foreign word,2 it makes an easy, memorable image with the meaning, and it is unique, so no two words share one. It can even be a phrase: "Pierre is sick" for the Russian3 persik, peach.

  1. Say the word aloud. The method runs on sound, not spelling, so hear it first.
  2. Find a keyword that sounds like any part of it: the start, the middle or the end. Concrete nouns are easiest to picture.
  3. Make the keyword and the meaning interact, with the levers from Vivid Images: action, size, a touch of the absurd.
  4. Use each keyword once. Two words sharing a keyword will blur together.
  5. Test in both directions. Cover the meanings and recall them from the Spanish, then cover the Spanish and recall it from the meanings.
Drill Learn these eight Spanish words. In brackets is the keyword Raugh and Atkinson's team used; swap in your own if it strikes you more. The quiz will ask what they mean.
  1. gusano (goose): worm
  2. tenedor (ten-door): fork
  3. maleta (mallet): suitcase
  4. payaso (pie): clown
  5. hilo (eel): thread
  6. trigo (tree): wheat
  7. jabón (bone): soap
  8. lagartija (log): lizard

Do not skip step 5. The Russian experiment tested one direction only: a Russian word was pronounced and learners typed the English.4 The keyword gives you only part of the foreign sound, so expect the reverse direction to need extra practice.

concepts.title: Myth check: a shortcut to fluency?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The keyword method is the fastest way to learn a language, so use it for everything.
Reality In their 2013 review of ten study techniques, Dunlosky and colleagues rated the keyword mnemonic low utility.1 In their words, it is difficult to implement in some contexts, and it appears to benefit students for a limited number of materials and for short retention intervals.2 The last point is debated: Atkinson and Raugh's keyword group was still well ahead six weeks later. A fair reading is that it is a strong tool for getting hard, concrete words in the door, and no substitute for listening, grammar and spaced testing.

Wait, really? A bad keyword can be worse than none. In one of Raugh and Atkinson's Spanish tests, most words were recalled far better with keywords, but not all. For libélula, dragonfly, with the keyword "bale", only 20 per cent of the keyword group got it right, against 60 per cent of the controls. For mosca, fly, keyword "Moscow", both groups scored 87 per cent: some words need no help at all. If a keyword keeps failing you, change it.

tryIt: Pick five words in a language you would like to learn, find a keyword that sounds like part of each, picture it with the meaning, and test yourself in both directions tomorrow.

title: Speeches and Poems Without Notes
description: Quintilian's advice on learning by heart, how actors learn lines, and a toast in eight beats

concepts.title: How it works: Quintilian's rules
concepts.contentHtml:
You have to give a five-minute speech at a wedding, and you would rather not read it off your phone. A Roman teacher of speakers faced the same problem, and most of his answers still hold.

Quintilian knew the system of places, in which the first thought is placed, as it were, in the forecourt of a house, the second in the living-room, and the rest in due order all round.1 But his own precepts, he said, were simpler:

  • Learn a long speech piecemeal, since there is nothing so bad for the memory as being overburdened,2 but not in sections so short that they break it up.
  • Use structure. Correct division, he wrote, will be an absolute safeguard against error in the order of our speech.3
  • Learn from the same tablets you wrote on, so the mind's eye can follow the lines, and mark the difficult passages with signs.
  • Use your voice, but keep it subdued, rising scarcely above a murmur.4
  • Test yourself instead of rereading, so you waste no time repeating passages you already know by heart.5

He also noticed something he could not explain. It is a curious fact, he wrote, that the interval of a single night will greatly increase the strength of the memory:6 things that could not be recalled on the spot are easily put together the next day. Whether to learn every word was, for him, a question of how much time and how good a memory you have. Given both, he would not let a single syllable escape. If time presses, it is far safer to secure a good grasp of the facts themselves and to leave yourself free to speak.7

concepts.title: Drill: a toast in eight beats
concepts.contentHtml:
Quintilian's ideal was a speech so well learned that it sounded like the inspiration of the moment.1 A speaker groping for memorised words, he warned, loses all the grace that a well-written speech can give.2 Most speeches do not need to be word-perfect, so learn the opening and closing lines exactly, and carry the middle as a chain of beats.

  1. Write it, then cut it into beats: one idea each, in the order they come.
  2. Give each beat an image with the levers from Vivid Images.
  3. Place the images along a route you know, such as the walk from your front door to your kitchen, one per stop, as Quintilian's orators did with the rooms of a house.
  4. Learn the first and last lines word for word, a section at a time, testing yourself rather than rereading.
  5. Rehearse aloud, on your feet, moving as you will on the day.
  6. Sleep on it, then run it once more the next day without notes.
Drill Here are the eight beats of a toast for a friend's fortieth birthday. Give each an image and place it on your route, in order. The quiz will ask for the order.
  1. Thank everyone for coming
  2. How you met: a broken-down bus
  3. The camping trip in the rain
  4. Her first terrible car
  5. The move to Glasgow
  6. The famous burnt lasagne
  7. What she means to her friends
  8. Raise your glasses

concepts.title: Myth check: in the first place
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The phrase "in the first place" is a fossil of the memory palace: listeners knew the speaker was walking through the rooms in his head.
Reality It is a lovely story, and it gets repeated as fact, for example in a 2013 essay by Gopal Sarma posted to arXiv.1 But it comes with no evidence, and there is a simpler explanation. Latin already used primo loco for "in the first place, first in order": Lewis and Short's Latin dictionary cites it from the satirist Juvenal. And English uses "place" for a position in an order anyway, as in first place in a race. Verdict: possible, but unproven.
Myth Actors learn their lines by saying them over and over.
Reality Professional actors recall text word for word using a meaning-based strategy, the kind that usually leaves only the gist.2 When Noice and Noice had actors think aloud while studying a script, they paid minute attention to the exact wording, even the punctuation, to work out the deep meaning they needed to perform it.3 In 2001 the same researchers found that even nonactors who read a script aloud while moving as a director instructed retained more than people who deliberately memorised it.4

Wait, really? The Noices also recorded the mnemonist Harry Lorayne, from lesson 2, thinking aloud as he learned the same script. His strategy was built on images and was totally different from the actors', yet both appeared to depend on the same underlying processes,5 and he had devised his own variation capable of verbatim retention. And what actors learn lasts: they rendered their scripts with about 98 per cent accuracy in performance,6 and three months after the final show they still recalled about 90 per cent.7

tryIt: Pick a short poem or toast, learn it in sections one evening, sleep on it, and recite it the next day without notes.
